Dimetrodon was a synapsid pelycosaur that thrived during the Permian period, about 295-275 years ago.

Although these majestic finned predators are often lumped in with dinosaurs, they're actually not related to Dinosauria, nor are they related to modern birds, snakes and lizards, or turtles. As a synapsid, they're actually closer to the ancestors of mammals. Although Dimetrodon and its relatives were not directly ancestral to the Mammalia, they're phylogenetically much closer to us than to dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus Rex.

Although Dimetrodon could technically be classified as a "reptile," its ancestors diverged very long ago from the ancestors of lizards or turtles. There's more phylogenetic diversity among extinct reptiles than you might expect, especially during the early radiation of these amniotic-egg-laying groups of animals. Pelycosaurs are synapsids, having only one temperal fenestra. Diapsids, like modern lizards and snakes, have two temporal fenestrae. Turtles are basically anapsid, but their evolutionary origins are still somewhat unclear, and fossil evidence can often be found to contradict molecular biological evidence.

Our ancestors aren't Dimetrodon, edaphosaurus, or any other sailed pelycosaur. Mammals actually derived from therapsids, another branch on the synapsid family tree. Therapsids are ugly as sin.

This has been a Paleontology FunFact about dimetrodons.
Paleontology FunFact: Dimetrodon is more closely related to extant mammals than to any living reptiles.

Any suggestions/experiences with low cost cameras?

(Sorry if this has been answered before, don't want to upset anyone!)
I have a small budget, camera help?
Even point-and-shoots make good pictures if you do it right.
Maybe an old film camera. Canon AE-1

You can probably find a used Olympus E-PL1 with kit lens on eBay for more or less your budget. It's a micro 4/3 sensor, so it would have better image quality than a point-and-shoot or smartphone camera.

You can do full manual control, so that's good for learning basic camera functions.

A used canon s90/95. It's cheap and has manual controls without sacrificing image quality for being a small point and shoot. Or, honestly, if you have a cell phone camera, just use that and spend the money on some books from your favorite photographers and study them.

A basic camera is all you need, don't get distracted by the bells and whistles. In fact basic can make you a better photographer because you have to learn to look at light and focus yourself instead of having a machine that will fix everything for you. I've met a lot of people that thought they were the bees knees in photography and when I handed them a film camera they discovered they had no idea what they were doing, the camera was doing all the work for them and they were just pushing a button. It's humbling.

I started film school and finished with the same canon rebel. My skill increased and I took better pictures, there was no need to upgrade until I started shooting roller derby and then I actually did need something with better ISO quality because of the lighting situations. But my advice to you is to find something used that you can put on manual. That is honestly all you need as far as equipment. The rest comes from you.

You can pick up a Nikon COOLPIX L120 14.1 MP for under $100 used on Amazon. It would be a great starter camera. There is so much to learn about photography and most of it can be learned with any simple camera.

Check your local www.usedwhatever.com site. I have purchased 3 very nice pocket cameras (2 Canon PowerShots and 1 Nikon CoolPix) via my local Kijiji site that all include aperture priority, shutter priority, and full manual modes - each for under $50 and each makes very good images. Don't get hung up on the megapixel idea, unless you are processing poster sized images 10 or 12 megapixels is quite enough :-) The very first image I sold at a gallery auction was taken with an ancient 7.1 megapixel A710 PowerShot - I still use it.

Dependent upon the type of photography you are interested in these cameras are good because they free you from "the bag".... that bulky thing you carry your camera, spare batteries, and extra lenses around in that is often more trouble than it's worth compared to reaching in your jacket pocket for a PowerShot.

As others have noted the Canon Rebel series is a very nice starter and beyond camera - I started with one about 5 years ago and even though I now have a full frame 5D the rebel is the most often used of the two.

You'll get more out of it if you know what you want and why you are doing it. Source: An Ivy Leaguer and PhD who believes that means fuck all.

My son was one of the smartest kids in his school, he got a place in a top uni and was very buoyed by it but at the end of that tough year he found that he wasn't the smartest, he was in a class where everyone was smart, he was just another number.

After struggling the first year the second got better, then the third, he didn't want to take a transition year because he'd seen others get summer jobs and once they got used to a bit of money in their pocket they never went back.

My son graduated in computer science, though it'd be a breeze to get a job but the old catch 22 went against him, need someone with experience, can't get experience without a job. He eventually got a job as an intern but was offered full time employment after 2 months and has been doing well since.

College is tough, but life after it is tougher. If you don't like doing what you are doing then become a barber, my father once said to me, do something people will always need a service for, as long as cars are on the road there'll be a need for mechanics, as long as people grow hair there'll always be a need for barbers.

Sorry this is so long winded but my message is as it was for my son, stick with it but if it's not for you then do something that will make you happy and not miserable. Best of luck for the future.

I suggest you finish some college degree, no matter the major, before you switch to barbering. HR departments are lazy and will set a hard requirement for having at least a bachelor's degree despite the fact that the position may not need it.

Let's say you stick it out and get the degree, now you get a job; that you probably dislike or hate. Then you get married, take on more debt, etc. Now you are trapped and can't quit to do what you want. Better to stop right now and avoid all of that.
